ranking.title: From Playtester to Imp at Infocom
ranking.excerpt: I have a very first person narrative view of the whole experience. Yeah, I can't tell you what it was like in a third person world. I don't really know what was happening to the for the other people and I have learned later that apparently there was this sense of we were the very clickish in group the imp the clickish of the clicks and the testers were on the outer margins of that and you know moving out in groups but it didn't it didn't feel that way so much to to us. So from my experience we had gone through the layoffs the Cornerstone disaster the purchase of of infocom by Activision and uh Steve came to me. I was one of his testers and he came to me some Saturday morning and said you know Amy you I think I had told him it would be a goal someday to be an imperson. It was sort of in the blue sky. ranking.title: Balancing Reality and Fiction in Games
ranking.excerpt: Um earlier I wanted to say when when asking about Steve giving advice, he may not have needed to give advice because I had read him in a at the time I was working there. I read his an interview with him. I think it was may have been for Games Magazine that that struck me at the time and and I still obviously remember it today which is he said there's this fine line with with reality and with setting up how the games how the rooms are described. He said, "If you if you say you walk into an office, there's a desk there. The player is going to expect the whole world of things that are on a typical desk, a stapler, a phone, you know, a pencil cup. Who knows what they're going to expect?" And you don't want to waste your time as a as an implementer coding in every single possible thing that could possibly be on a desktop when what you really only care about is, you know, the magic pen that's in the pencil cup. Um, whereas if you say you walk into a wizard's uh lab or a wizard's cave, who knows what's in a wizard's cave. So you can get away with a lot by setting it in this fantasy at environment that people don't have predetermined expectations about what should be in that environment. Um, and and so I think that's some of what you're talking about of of at the level of the ters's job was not just to find bugs. the rather dull QA of where does the computer crash. It's where does the world that you've invented break down and what is a reasonable approximation of things that are on the desk. Let's say that people will look for without having to burden the code with everything possible. And you could argue that in Plundered Hearts I didn't I didn't broaden it enough. I didn't get enough of those because people were complaining you can't karate chop or or things. Um, certainly I know I'm still embarrassed to this day in the final released version there's a bug that happens in the first couple moves, when you do something very logical and I can't remember what it is right now but it then that's a it's a true bug. You get garbage if you type out something like take the box there's a box under the bed that slides out and if you take the box rather than grab the box or something that's a logical thing to do you get garbage from it. So that was a case where the testers had missed or I missed in in my own I should take responsibility a very obvious thing to have done at the beginning.

I think some of what made Infocom so great was this individual vision that they were able to that the style of the game and the ability with a text adventure. It's you know it's it is a book. I'll I'll go strongly. It is a book just done a little differently. You get an individual vision in a different way than you do when you're having to hire voice uh what do they call voice actors. you know, Mark Hamill has to be in this and we got to have graphics and we got to have certain algorithms for the fight scenes and things. ranking.title: Creating a Romance Game for Women
ranking.excerpt: That was I will take the credit and the blame. I think that was all my idea. I mean, I think they were fine with me going forward with it. And it wasn't that there hadn't been women writing text adventures before. Um, even in our company, though they hadn't been, you know, the main imp. Um, but I think it was a good selling point of, oh, look, and there was this movement at that time. is before Brenda Laurel and before I think it's Purple Moon, which has gone out of business now, but the games for girls, the games that they were coming out for girls at that time were like cooking games. Oh, let's have a sewing game and which is just benited. It it just the concept that and they weren't fun to play either. Um so, no wonder girls weren't interested in playing them. I'm not actually going to claim that Plundered Hearts is a game that girls would be that interested in playing because I think the mode of play is something that developmentally teenage girls aren't that interested in doing sitting down with a computer by yourself. I think Brenda Laurel and some other companies have done good ways of of getting games that girls will be interested in playing. But we didn't know that then. And I was interested in in writing romance. I thought a romance might be kind of fun and different. And it had this, you know, this gimmick of a woman writing for women. So there were at the time there were some critical reviews that just hated it because of its over femininess. And I remember one reviewer just lit into the game because she was trying to karate chop and to do tough guy stuff and the game wouldn't let her. And so she was criticizing it for not allowing uh the character to be strong. And we can go into a whole sort of philosophical approach about what a character should be in one of these games.

ranking.title: Commercial Pressures and Romance Games
ranking.excerpt: No, no, it was very very clear. I think they would have been happier for me not to have done Romance game first. It's not like I railroaded them into it. But I think there was there was definitely hey let's do something for women, you know, so we can do the whole women writing for women. We can get that whole new market 'cuz it was definitely at the time the whole time I was essentially after my first six months at Infocom, it was all the beginning of the end. And so there was a panic underlying everything of "where is the next Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy ?" and that's that would be my anger is after Plundered Hearts. He said, "Well, that's good. You know, you didn't sell very many, dear." It it wasn't quite that condescending, but it was almost was "just go out and just write us another game that will sell 150,000 copies", which none of the other games had done except for Hitchhogers, which still like 400,000 copies, you know. So, it was this impossible task that was laid on and oh, we don't want to burden you with with telling you what to do. Just you just write us a hit. And it was very frustrating for me because I had perhaps bitten off more than I could chew with my first game and trying a different genre and... ...a different play, a type of play for an entirely new market that then, you know, again, this is something I don't know a lot about cuz I was kind of the innocent newbie throughout the whole experience. But from what I was told at the time, sales didn't know what to do with Activision sales didn't know what to do with the Infocom games. are sold to a slightly different market, a different kind of player. Um, it's a very different kind of play at the time. Um, you know, sitting down for 100, 150 hours with the game was not the same as Pong, you know. So, it was I could I could blame the lack of sales on things far beyond my ability to to control. Um but it also probably was being marketed to the wrong group and the people who would been interested weren't interested in playing computer games. So marketing was not unaware of that to to bring it back to the question which is no they did not say here sit down you have to write a game a romance. So, I think they played on that after the fact to have something to talk about, you know, about the game, but I don't even remember what else I had in mind for the first game. Um, I had in high school uh thought I would write romance novels when I was going to be a grown-up. So, so writing a romance seemed to be a a logical thing to do and something different. But no, it did not come from outside.

ranking.title: Balancing Reality and Fiction in Games
ranking.excerpt: Um earlier I wanted to say when when asking about Steve giving advice, he may not have needed to give advice because I had read him in a at the time I was working there. I read his an interview with him. I think it was may have been for Games Magazine that that struck me at the time and and I still obviously remember it today which is he said there's this fine line with with reality and with setting up how the games how the rooms are described. He said, "If you if you say you walk into an office, there's a desk there. The player is going to expect the whole world of things that are on a typical desk, a stapler, a phone, you know, a pencil cup. Who knows what they're going to expect?" And you don't want to waste your time as a as an implementer coding in every single possible thing that could possibly be on a desktop when what you really only care about is, you know, the magic pen that's in the pencil cup. Um, whereas if you say you walk into a wizard's uh lab or a wizard's cave, who knows what's in a wizard's cave. So you can get away with a lot by setting it in this fantasy at environment that people don't have predetermined expectations about what should be in that environment. Um, and and so I think that's some of what you're talking about of of at the level of the ters's job was not just to find bugs. the rather dull QA of where does the computer crash. It's where does the world that you've invented break down and what is a reasonable approximation of things that are on the desk. Let's say that people will look for without having to burden the code with everything possible. And you could argue that in Plundered Hearts I didn't I didn't broaden it enough. I didn't get enough of those because people were complaining you can't karate chop or or things. Um, certainly I know I'm still embarrassed to this day in the final released version there's a bug that happens in the first couple moves, when you do something very logical and I can't remember what it is right now but it then that's a it's a true bug. You get garbage if you type out something like take the box there's a box under the bed that slides out and if you take the box rather than grab the box or something that's a logical thing to do you get garbage from it. So that was a case where the testers had missed or I missed in in my own I should take responsibility a very obvious thing to have done at the beginning.

ranking.title: Organisation and Culture Among the Imps
ranking.excerpt: So, we had a you'd walk into reception with marketing and then beyond that into you you go gez you can go to the right and go to the imps go to the left and you get to the testing area and go further to the left and around the building you'd be where they developed the parser and Tim Anderson and the the guys who I considered the real programmers work. I misspoke. not the parts are the interpreters were written over there and then administration the big guys were down the hall by themselves in a corner. Um, and the imps area has probably been described we we had what we called a bowling alley. It was a very large open room with windows at the end and it was on the corner of the building. So, all of the imps on the north side had windows in their offices with John Palace on the corner and then a big series of windows for the bowling alley and then a line of offices on the south side with Steve Moritzky had the southside windowed office and then the rest of us had the closedin offices on the south side. And we did talk about the north side kids and the southside kids. And the north side were the real programmers and the southside were the just the dabblers who had the creative ability and were struggling with the programming. That that was the myth because of course Steve was on the south side but he wasn't considered one of the real programmers and he didn't have a computer science degree. But he definitely in that deserved to be on the north side. I think he kind of enjoyed being on the south side. So the southside was me, Jeff O'Neal, and Hollywood, who actually was not on the southside, it was on the what would east side, but it was also a windowless office. Um I think the intent had been to when we got up and running and were famous, assuming they even were going to have games, that there would be cubicles in the center of that big area and then we'd have games just routing out our ears from all the people working all at once. So, you'd show up when you'd show up. I don't remember ever being rushed, and I'm not a morning person, so I don't think it was an an early time. Um, I would the doors were always open. Um, except in few cases when people didn't want to be bothered, but it was actually a really wonderful way to work. all of the imps, we were all working on our own projects separately, but in a shared environment and and for me it was a it was a great it was kind of the perfect environment because you had the team the sense of we're all working together on something but I didn't have to share my work with anybody else. There was no need to actually work with partners. Other people work well with partners. I don't but I had the team support without the individual butting in

ranking.title: Imps' Lunches and a Supportive Atmosphere
ranking.excerpt: Um, and at the imps lunches it was a supportive atmosphere. I don't recall I mean I know there must have been fights between imps and I know that there were fights between imps but I don't recall anything at these lunches among us except sort of support of gez you know I've got a puzzle I can't figure out how to solve it. It's boring. how do we solve this puzzle or how do I we didn't do coding questions because it's sitting around a lunch table is not a good place to do coding uh problem solving. So that wasn't the kind of thing we discussed that you'd walk over to Stu Stu Galley is usually the person I'd check in with. I mean depended what what you were looking for. Stu was the person I go to for parser stuff. Leveling for really complex stuff in programming. Steve for real questions for comedy, you know, how to make something funny. Um or just how to get out of a pickle in the story. Um, and then at the in lunches, it was all just a free-for-all of people talking and suggesting. Um so that would pretty much be how how it would work. It was everybody working on their own thing but together.

ranking.title: A Young Company of Passionate Developers
ranking.excerpt: So the other side of it was again from my experience from within the whole company we were all very young. I was younger than the average, but I was like 22, 23. Um, but but and the guys, somebody can tell you what the average age, there's a t-shirt that was given to the first person who would age, the oldest person in the company, you know. So, it was a young company. We all, most of us were single. We would just live there. It was our our home and our family as well as our workplace. So, for me to write a game, I would just work. I' get into work to test, you know, at 9:00, 9:30, 10:00. I'd work till 6:30 or 7:00 and then I'd work on the game for 2 or 3 hours. Go out to dinner with somebody, you know, else who was working late, come back. The company was open and there all the time. And then I worked all weekends when I was sort of actively in the mindset of I'm going to be coming in. I have to do this. I was getting up at six in the morning and coming in Saturdays and Sundays, too, to to write my game on the on the weekends when I wasn't working. But it wasn't hard. It was just part of the whole culture of the company. I was not alone in this is what I mean to say. You'd see other people there at the company, not writing their own games necessarily, but there to play games on the computers that we had available or to just hang out, everything. So, I guess in that way, it was probably different from other places I've worked.

ranking.title: An Absurd Wonderland for Playtesting
ranking.excerpt: Um, I had written a really off-the-wall, bizarre little game that came from who knows where about being a tester in a sort of Alice in Wonderland alternate dimension and taking your your bugs, which are real metamorphosized bugs, to the imp who was like a caterpillar at a hookah. you know, it was very bizarre and didn't and it esc got around all of the real world things of like rope so that my test game that I had done to sort of prove I could do it didn't have any warning signals. Um, I mean, I would talk with all of the guys about I mean it was sort of an open atmosphere for some of us. So, it was up to the individual imp how much he wanted to share with the others, but I would ask about puzzle problems and and things, but I don't remember any any uh advice on that level. I know that that Steve did help me decide what to after I was hired, what what should my first game be, and I talked with it with him about it fairly often. Um, and I do remember him saying he would not have done Plundered Hearts first. I mean, before I started, he said, "This is not what I do for my first game because it sounds too hard." and I didn't take his advice on that. But so so obviously there was there was mentoring and discussion going on, but I don't remember specifics like that.

ranking.excerpt: That was I will take the credit and the blame. I think that was all my idea. I mean, I think they were fine with me going forward with it. And it wasn't that there hadn't been women writing text adventures before. Um, even in our company, though they hadn't been, you know, the main imp. Um, but I think it was a good selling point of, oh, look, and there was this movement at that time. is before Brenda Laurel and before I think it's Purple Moon, which has gone out of business now, but the games for girls, the games that they were coming out for girls at that time were like cooking games. Oh, let's have a sewing game and which is just benited. It it just the concept that and they weren't fun to play either. Um so, no wonder girls weren't interested in playing them. I'm not actually going to claim that Plundered Hearts is a game that girls would be that interested in playing because I think the mode of play is something that developmentally teenage girls aren't that interested in doing sitting down with a computer by yourself. I think Brenda Laurel and some other companies have done good ways of of getting games that girls will be interested in playing. But we didn't know that then. And I was interested in in writing romance. I thought a romance might be kind of fun and different. And it had this, you know, this gimmick of a woman writing for women. So there were at the time there were some critical reviews that just hated it because of its over femininess. And I remember one reviewer just lit into the game because she was trying to karate chop and to do tough guy stuff and the game wouldn't let her. And so she was criticizing it for not allowing uh the character to be strong. And we can go into a whole sort of philosophical approach about what a character should be in one of these games.

ranking.title: Commercial Pressures and Romance Games
ranking.excerpt: No, no, it was very very clear. I think they would have been happier for me not to have done Romance game first. It's not like I railroaded them into it. But I think there was there was definitely hey let's do something for women, you know, so we can do the whole women writing for women. We can get that whole new market 'cuz it was definitely at the time the whole time I was essentially after my first six months at Infocom, it was all the beginning of the end. And so there was a panic underlying everything of "where is the next Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy ?" and that's that would be my anger is after Plundered Hearts. He said, "Well, that's good. You know, you didn't sell very many, dear." It it wasn't quite that condescending, but it was almost was "just go out and just write us another game that will sell 150,000 copies", which none of the other games had done except for Hitchhogers, which still like 400,000 copies, you know. So, it was this impossible task that was laid on and oh, we don't want to burden you with with telling you what to do. Just you just write us a hit. And it was very frustrating for me because I had perhaps bitten off more than I could chew with my first game and trying a different genre and... ...a different play, a type of play for an entirely new market that then, you know, again, this is something I don't know a lot about cuz I was kind of the innocent newbie throughout the whole experience. But from what I was told at the time, sales didn't know what to do with Activision sales didn't know what to do with the Infocom games. are sold to a slightly different market, a different kind of player. records.text: The office was also a home and social circle, where working late did not mean being alone.

ranking.title: A Young Company of Passionate Developers
ranking.excerpt: So the other side of it was again from my experience from within the whole company we were all very young. I was younger than the average, but I was like 22, 23. Um, but but and the guys, somebody can tell you what the average age, there's a t-shirt that was given to the first person who would age, the oldest person in the company, you know. So, it was a young company. We all, most of us were single. We would just live there. It was our our home and our family as well as our workplace. So, for me to write a game, I would just work. I' get into work to test, you know, at 9:00, 9:30, 10:00. I'd work till 6:30 or 7:00 and then I'd work on the game for 2 or 3 hours. Go out to dinner with somebody, you know, else who was working late, come back. The company was open and there all the time. And then I worked all weekends when I was sort of actively in the mindset of I'm going to be coming in. I have to do this. I was getting up at six in the morning and coming in Saturdays and Sundays, too, to to write my game on the on the weekends when I wasn't working. But it wasn't hard. It was just part of the whole culture of the company. I was not alone in this is what I mean to say. You'd see other people there at the company, not writing their own games necessarily, but there to play games on the computers that we had available or to just hang out, everything. So, I guess in that way, it was probably different from other places I've worked.

ranking.title: Organisation and Culture Among the Imps
ranking.excerpt: So, we had a you'd walk into reception with marketing and then beyond that into you you go gez you can go to the right and go to the imps go to the left and you get to the testing area and go further to the left and around the building you'd be where they developed the parser and Tim Anderson and the the guys who I considered the real programmers work. I misspoke. not the parts are the interpreters were written over there and then administration the big guys were down the hall by themselves in a corner. Um, and the imps area has probably been described we we had what we called a bowling alley. It was a very large open room with windows at the end and it was on the corner of the building. So, all of the imps on the north side had windows in their offices with John Palace on the corner and then a big series of windows for the bowling alley and then a line of offices on the south side with Steve Moritzky had the southside windowed office and then the rest of us had the closedin offices on the south side. And we did talk about the north side kids and the southside kids. And the north side were the real programmers and the southside were the just the dabblers who had the creative ability and were struggling with the programming. That that was the myth because of course Steve was on the south side but he wasn't considered one of the real programmers and he didn't have a computer science degree. But he definitely in that deserved to be on the north side. I think he kind of enjoyed being on the south side. So the southside was me, Jeff O'Neal, and Hollywood, who actually was not on the southside, it was on the what would east side, but it was also a windowless office. Um I think the intent had been to when we got up and running and were famous, assuming they even were going to have games, that there would be cubicles in the center of that big area and then we'd have games just routing out our ears from all the people working all at once. So, you'd show up when you'd show up. I don't remember ever being rushed, and I'm not a morning person, so I don't think it was an an early time. Um, I would the doors were always open. Um, except in few cases when people didn't want to be bothered, but it was actually a really wonderful way to work. all of the imps, we were all working on our own projects separately, but in a shared environment and and for me it was a it was a great it was kind of the perfect environment because you had the team the sense of we're all working together on something but I didn't have to share my work with anybody else. There was no need to actually work with partners. Other people work well with partners. I don't but I had the team support without the individual butting in

ranking.excerpt: Um, and at the imps lunches it was a supportive atmosphere. I don't recall I mean I know there must have been fights between imps and I know that there were fights between imps but I don't recall anything at these lunches among us except sort of support of gez you know I've got a puzzle I can't figure out how to solve it. It's boring. how do we solve this puzzle or how do I we didn't do coding questions because it's sitting around a lunch table is not a good place to do coding uh problem solving. So that wasn't the kind of thing we discussed that you'd walk over to Stu Stu Galley is usually the person I'd check in with. I mean depended what what you were looking for. Stu was the person I go to for parser stuff. Leveling for really complex stuff in programming. Steve for real questions for comedy, you know, how to make something funny. Um or just how to get out of a pickle in the story. Um, and then at the in lunches, it was all just a free-for-all of people talking and suggesting. Um so that would pretty much be how how it would work. It was everybody working on their own thing but together.
